learningObjective: Explain why the Halide paper separates the algorithm (what to compute) from the schedule (how to compute) and identify the design intent behind this separation.

canonicalClaims.claim: Halide separates the declarative algorithm from the imperative schedule so that a single, portable algorithm can be re-scheduled (tiled, vectorized, parallelized, fused, recomputed) without changing its meaning, enabling non-expert programmers to explore many performance-relevant strategies without rewriting the pipeline and allowing schedules to be tuned per target architecture.
conditions: The algorithm is expressed as a set of pure functions with dependencies but no explicit loop nesting.
The schedule expresses loop nesting, tiling, storage granularity, and computation-vs-storage trade-offs.
The compiler is responsible for lowering the (algorithm, schedule) pair into equivalent imperative code.
nonImplications: Does not imply that a schedule can violate dependencies; only choices that preserve algorithm semantics are legal.
Does not imply that any schedule is beneficial — most schedules are worse than the naive one; the point is that many alternatives can be tried cheaply.

misconceptions.claim: Halide's separation exists to hide the algorithm from the user so that only compiler-generated schedules are visible.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The paper's stated goal is exactly the opposite: to expose scheduling choices to programmers as a first-class, portable knob, while keeping the algorithm concise and readable.

misconceptions.claim: The separation is a compiler-implementation convenience with no user-facing significance; users always write both parts together as a monolithic function.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The user writes algorithm and schedule as separate constructs; the paper argues that this separation is the key design contribution.

misconceptions.claim: Halide's schedule can change the algorithm's output values (e.g. approximate results) to gain speed; the schedule is thus a form of lossy transformation.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Legal Halide schedules preserve algorithmic semantics; they never change output values, only the order/granularity of computation and storage.
